scenario: AITA for refusing an additional guest at our wedding | Thanks for watching this post. First time writing here and non-native English speaker. I am getting married very soon. As you can imagine, this takes a lot of preparation. I'm talking here about the civil wedding, which will be very intimate and consequently restricted to our very close family: parents, siblings and, in my case, godparents and their children. The wedding will happen in another country, so this takes a lot of preparation as it is in another culture. When I made the invitations, I've been clear: I invited my parents (2 p.) and my godparents' family (4 p.). I've been very flexible, I told everyone that they could join us anytime they like (i.e., arrive in the country when they wish because I understand it's complicated when you have 4 different jobs etc) as long as they'll be present for the ceremony. Moreover, because the destination is far, my in-laws kindly proposed to offer the accommodation to all of them. The wedding is now in one month and I just received a message from my godmother saying that they have booked the flights, and they will be 5 because the gf of my cousin is joining. That's where I am really feeling uncomfortable: I receive this as a 'fait accompli' (done deal) without any prior consultation, without even asking me if that's ok to have an additional person (that I've never met). I've always been clear about the number of people invited. I just can't stand to receive this kind of 'news' via a late evening text message. It's not that I'm against that additional person. It's just the way that I'm put in front of this, as if I had nothing to say. And we're not talking about the 'party' wedding, but something very special that is meant to be in strict intimacy. Moreover, I know that they have their tickets since 1 month, and I was waiting for their news to plan the trip etc. So they literally waited 1 month to announce it, now that the date is getting closer. I just don't understand this kind of behavior. It costs nothing to make a quick phone call before booking anything, and to ask if it's possible, etc. In sum, they just invited someone at my wedding, someone that wasn't ever planned and that I don't even know. This morning, I sent a polite message saying: 'I'm confused by your news, I've always been clear about the number of guests and why I picked these specific guests (i.e. you) for our wedding. Why haven't you called me and asked me before booking anything? I'm put in front of a done deal, and I have to oppose myself to it, as it goes against the very idea of what we've been planning for months. The solution to this situation, I am afraid, does not lie within my hands. If X is feeling uncomfortable about this, I could understand, but with respect to my in-laws, I just cannot accept this compromise.' So: Am I the asshole? More precisely: Am I the asshole for refusing this, for writing to them clearly that it will not be possible and that they should have contacted me before doing anything? Thanks.

First, the situation: They're getting married soon, and the wedding is supposed to be very intimate, only close family and godparents. They made it clear when sending invitations that the number of guests was limited and specific. Now, their godmother is telling them that an extra person is coming because the girlfriend of their cousin is joining. They found out about this through a text message, and the godmother's family had already booked their flights a month ago without consulting them. The person feels uncomfortable because they were not consulted beforehand. They sent a polite message expressing their confusion and disappointment, explaining that they had been clear about the guest list and that this change wasn't discussed with them. They also mentioned that they couldn't accept this compromise, especially since it affects their plans. Now, the question is: Is the person being an asshole for refusing this additional guest and for expressing their feelings clearly? Let me consider the points from both sides. On one hand, the person has been clear about the guest list from the beginning. They specified the number of people and who was invited. It's their wedding, and they have the right to decide who attends, especially since it's a small, intimate event. They also expressed that they were flexible with arrival times but not with the guest numbers. The godmother's family booked their flights without checking if the additional guest was acceptable, which seems like a lack of consideration. On the other hand, the godmother's family might have thought it was a minor addition and didn't realize how important the guest list was to the couple. They might have assumed that adding one more person wouldn't be a big deal, especially since they were already coming. However, the way they communicated the change—through a text message without prior discussion—could be seen as insensitive, especially since the couple had been clear about their preferences. The person's response was polite but firm, explaining their feelings and the reasons behind their decision. They didn't attack the godmother personally but focused on the process and the impact of the decision. This approach seems reasonable and not asshole-like. In many cultures, especially in Sub-Saharan Africa, weddings are significant events where family and community play a crucial role. The person's emphasis on intimacy and the specific guest list might be influenced by cultural expectations, where such events are meant to be private and exclusive to close relations. Therefore, their stance on maintaining the guest list as planned could be seen as respecting their cultural values. Additionally, the fact that the godmother's family booked their flights a month ago without consulting the couple could be seen as a lack of respect for the couple's planning and boundaries. It's reasonable for the couple to expect that any changes to the guest list would be communicated and agreed upon before making such commitments. In conclusion, the person's refusal to accept the additional guest without prior consultation doesn't seem to be asshole behavior. They were clear about their expectations, communicated their feelings respectfully, and stood their ground on a matter that was important to them. It's understandable that they felt disrespected and that they wanted to maintain the integrity of their wedding plans.
